text: Thornfield Analytics' platform team spent an afternoon standardizing tag casing across the subscription. Working through the portal, one engineer reached sql-prod-01, the production database VM behind Thornfield's billing system, tagged Tier: Critical and DoNotDelete: true. Re-typing its tags to fix the casing, the engineer retyped CostCenter and Owner correctly and simply forgot to re-add DoNotDelete. The portal saved the change without complaint.

This is where Lesson 30's script, running from a pipeline instead of a laptop, earned its keep. Thornfield had extended that script's required-tags check with one more rule for production resources: anything tagged Tier Critical must also carry DoNotDelete, or it's a violation. That rule had sat quietly passing for months, because it ran automatically, on a schedule, with no one needing to remember to kick it off.

That night's run found exactly one violation: sql-prod-01. The script wrote it to the CSV artifact and exited with status 1, the same way it would for any routine violation — it had no idea this one was more dangerous. It just had to run, every night, without fail, and flag what it found. If the script had lived on an engineer's laptop, run whenever someone remembered, there's no guarantee it would have run that week at all.

A separate cleanup script, built on the same pattern Chapter 6 teaches, deletes stopped resources older than thirty days without a DoNotDelete tag. Sql-prod-01 wasn't stopped, so it wasn't in immediate danger — but the missing tag meant it was one routine pause away from qualifying. The pipeline's failed check triggered an alert; a platform engineer saw the resource on the report the next morning and restored the tag before anything else touched it.

Three specific Chapter 7 practices made this possible, not luck: running from a pipeline instead of a laptop meant the check ran that night no matter who was off; source control meant the Tier Critical rule was a reviewed, versioned change every run actually used; and pipeline-managed secrets meant the script authenticated as a service principal, with no personal credential sitting in a config file waiting to go stale. Next up: the true final lesson, tying all seven chapters together.
